ribeira-pontes.name: Ribeira and the Bridges
ribeira-pontes.subtitle: The old waterfront, the Luís I Bridge and the Gaia wine cellars
ribeira-pontes.description: The route starts on the Ribeira waterfront, among the colourful houses and the port-wine bars. Climb to the upper deck of the Luís I Bridge — the best viewpoint over the Douro. Cross the river to Gaia and walk down to Cais de Gaia, where the Sandeman, Graham’s and Taylor’s cellars line the quay: this is where port is tasted and explained. Ride the Teleférico de Gaia cable car back up to the bridge, and take the historic 1891 Guindais funicular down to the Ribeira. A cellar visit takes about two hours, so start in the morning to be back before sunset.

stops.note: A walk along the Ribeira waterfront: colourful façades, rabelo boats and Ribeira Negra square. The Luís I Bridge is visible from here.
Climb to the upper deck of the bridge. The pedestrian deck carries Gustave Eiffel’s 1886 iron arch; the view sweeps over the Ribeira and the Gaia cellars.
Cross the river and walk down to Cais de Gaia. A tour and tasting at one of the cellars (Sandeman, Graham’s, Taylor’s). The Teleférico de Gaia cable car takes you back up to the bridge.
Return over the upper deck of the bridge. At the Ribeira, ride the 1891 Guindais funicular down along the city wall to the bridge.

legs.note: From the waterfront uphill to the bridge span: by the Guindais steps or through Rua de Miragaia.
On foot across the upper deck of the Luís I Bridge over the Douro and down to Cais de Gaia.
Walk back over the upper deck; alternatively the Guindais funicular by the Ribeira.

baixa-historica.name: The Historic Baixa
baixa-historica.subtitle: São Bento, Aliados, Clérigos, Lello, Carmo, Bolhão, the Cathedral and the Exchange
baixa-historica.description: A walk through Porto’s historic centre. Start at São Bento station and look at the twenty thousand azulejos by Jorge Colaço in the hall. Climb through Avenida dos Aliados to the Clérigos church and tower for a view over the whole city, then step into Livraria Lello on Rua das Carmelitas. Carmo church stands opposite, across the street. Continue to Bolhão market for produce and snacks, Porto’s oldest cathedral on the hill, and the Palácio da Bolsa with its Arab Room. Watch the clock: Lello and the Exchange keep their own hours, and the market closes in the afternoon.

stops.note: The station hall with Jorge Colaço’s 1905–1906 azulejos: battle scenes and the history of transport.
Avenida dos Aliados with the city-hall façade and the bank. The pedestrian Rua das Flores begins here.
Niccolò Nasoni’s Clérigos church and tower. Climb the 1763 belfry — 225 steps and a panorama of the city.
The 1906 Livraria Lello with its red staircase and skylight. Entry is ticketed and deducted from a book purchase.
Carmo church opposite: a Baroque façade covered in blue-and-white azulejos.
Bolhão market, founded in 1834: fruit, cheese, fish and snacks. The perfect spot for lunch among locals.
The 12th-century Romanesque cathedral on the hill: Gothic cloister with azulejos and a terrace over the bishop’s palace.
The Palácio da Bolsa on a guided tour: the glass-roofed Nations’ Courtyard and the gilded Arab Room in the style of the Alhambra.
The Gothic church of São Francisco, with Porto’s most lavish gilded Baroque interior and its catacombs.

legs.note: From the station down the street to Avenida dos Aliados.
Through pedestrian Rua das Flores and the square to the Clérigos.
A couple of minutes to Rua das Carmelitas.
Carmo stands directly opposite, across the street.
East to Bolhão market beside the Conceição church.
Uphill to the cathedral on the Terreiro da Sé.
Down to Infante Henry square and the Palácio da Bolsa.
A few steps to the church of São Francisco.

douro-oceano.name: The Douro and the Ocean
douro-oceano.subtitle: Tram 1 along the river from the Ribeira to the Felgueiras lighthouse
douro-oceano.description: The historic tram 1 runs from the Ribeira along the right bank of the Douro through Miragaia and Massarelos. It is the city’s most scenic route: the river and bridges on one side, façades and gardens on the other. Get off at the climb to the Palácio de Cristal and wander the terraces above the Douro. Then take the tram again to Lordelo and Foz, a short walk from the Serralves Foundation with its Álvaro Siza museum and park. Finish at the Felgueiras lighthouse, where the Douro meets the Atlantic. Tram 1 runs about every 20–30 minutes; check the timetable in advance, especially out of season.

stops.note: Board tram 1 at the Ribeira (Infante stop). Historic cars from the 1920s–1930s.
The tram passes Massarelos. Get off by the Palácio de Cristal: terraces and gardens above the Douro, with a panorama of the river and bridges.
Continue by tram to Lordelo / Foz. The Serralves Foundation: Álvaro Siza museum, Art Deco villa and contemporary park.
Tram to the Foz terminus, then walk to the Felgueiras lighthouse. The mouth of the Douro, the ocean horizon and sunset.

legs.note: Tram 1 (E1) along the Douro through Miragaia and Massarelos to the climb by the Palácio de Cristal.
Back on tram 1 to Foz / Lordelo; then on foot to the Serralves Foundation and park.
Tram 1 to the Foz terminus (Passeio Alegre), then on foot to the Felgueiras lighthouse.

gaia-vinho.name: Gaia and Port Wine
gaia-vinho.subtitle: The Ribeira, the Luís I Bridge, Serra do Pilar and the Cais de Gaia lodges
gaia-vinho.description: The route begins at the Ribeira and leads to the other bank of the Douro. Climb to the upper deck of the Luís I Bridge and walk across to the monastery of Serra do Pilar — a 16th-century round church and the best viewpoint over Porto. From there ride the Teleférico de Gaia cable car down to the Cais de Gaia waterfront, where the wine lodges stand. A tour with tasting in one of them (Sandeman, Graham’s, Taylor’s) takes about an hour and a half. You can return over the bridge or by cable car. Start in the morning: the lodges get busy, and you will want to be back at the viewpoint by sunset.

stops.note: A walk along the Ribeira waterfront: colourful façades, rabelo boats and arcaded houses. The Luís I Bridge is visible from here.
Climb to the upper deck of the Luís I Bridge and walk across the Douro to the Gaia side. The bridge opens a panorama of the Ribeira and the lodges.
The 16th-century monastery of Serra do Pilar, with its round domed church and cloister gallery. The viewpoint takes in the whole of Porto.
Ride the Teleférico de Gaia cable car down to the Cais de Gaia waterfront. Old rabelo boats and wine warehouses line the river.
A tour and tasting at the Sandeman, Graham’s or Taylor’s lodges. Here they explain how port is aged and how the styles differ.

legs.note: From the Ribeira uphill to the bridge span: by the Guindais steps or through Rua de Miragaia.
On foot across the upper deck of the Luís I Bridge over the Douro and up to the monastery of Serra do Pilar.
Down by the Teleférico de Gaia cable car (Jardim do Morro — Cais de Gaia); the route profile follows the streets of the hill.
A couple of minutes along the Cais de Gaia waterfront to the wine lodges.

igrejas-azulejos.name: Churches and Azulejos
igrejas-azulejos.subtitle: Cedofeita, Lapa, Carmo, Capela das Almas and Santo Ildefonso
igrejas-azulejos.description: A walking route through the churches of Porto whose Baroque façades are clad in blue-and-white azulejos. Begin at the Romanesque church of Cedofeita, the oldest in the city, then climb to the church of Lapa with its rich Baroque altar. Follow Rua das Carmelitas to the church of Carmo, whose side façade is entirely tiled, and to the Carmelite church opposite. Through Praça Guilherme Gomes Fernandes reach the Capela das Almas — Porto’s most recognisable tiled church — and finish at Santo Ildefonso, with its huge azulejo panel on the west front. The route is almost entirely on foot and suits a morning.

stops.note: The Romanesque church of Cedofeita, 11th–12th century — Porto’s oldest surviving church, rebuilt in Baroque style inside.
The church of Lapa with its rich Baroque altar and the brotherhood that adorned the church over the centuries.
The church of Carmo: its side façade is covered in blue-and-white azulejos, with the Carmelite church beside it.
The Capela das Almas on Rua de Santa Catarina: the façade is one continuous tile panel depicting scenes of the Passion.
The church of Santo Ildefonso with its huge azulejo panel on the west front, facing Praça da Batalha.

legs.note: From Cedofeita north to the church of Lapa.
Along Rua das Carmelitas south to the church of Carmo.
Through Praça Guilherme Gomes Fernandes to Rua de Santa Catarina.
A few minutes along Rua de Santa Catarina to Praça da Batalha.

museus-jardins.name: Museums and Gardens
museus-jardins.subtitle: Soares dos Reis, Casa do Infante, the Alfândega, Cordoaria and Parque da Cidade
museus-jardins.description: A route through the museums and greenery of Porto. Begin at the National Museum Soares dos Reis with Portuguese sculpture and painting, then descend to the river at the Casa do Infante — the house where Prince Henry is said to have been born. Follow the Douro to the Alfândega Nova, the former customs house and exhibition space, and climb to the Cordoaria, a former ropewalk with a square under old plane trees. The last stretch is by taxi or bus to Parque da Cidade, the large city park with lakes and dunes by the ocean. Go on a weekday: the museums close on Mondays, while the park is good any day.

stops.note: The National Museum Soares dos Reis: Portuguese sculpture and painting of the 19th–20th centuries in the Carrancas Palace.
The Casa do Infante, a 15th-century Gothic house where Prince Henry the Navigator is said to have been born; today it is the city museum.
The Alfândega Nova of 1860 — the former customs house with its iron structure, now an exhibition and museum centre on the Douro.
The Cordoaria, a former ropewalk, now a square under old plane trees beside the tower and the hospital.
Parque da Cidade — Porto’s largest park, with lakes, lawns and dunes reaching towards the Atlantic.

legs.note: From the Soares dos Reis museum down through the streets to the river and the Casa do Infante.
Along the Douro bank to the Alfândega Nova.
Uphill from the river to the Cordoaria.
The long leg by taxi or bus to Parque da Cidade; a bicycle along the river is another option.

matosinhos-mar.name: Matosinhos and the Sea
matosinhos-mar.subtitle: Parque da Cidade, the Matosinhos fish market and the Leça lighthouse
matosinhos-mar.description: The route heads north from Parque da Cidade towards the sea, along the coast that runs from Foz to Matosinhos and Leça da Palmeira. First the big city park with its lakes and dunes, then the Matosinhos fish market, where sardine and tuna are sold from early morning, and the town hall with its square. The last stretch follows the shore to the rocky point where the Leça lighthouse has shone since 1926, and beyond it the Atlantic opens. In Matosinhos be sure to try fresh grilled fish: dozens of restaurants by the port cook it straight from the morning catch. Tram 1 only reaches Foz; from there bus and metro line A continue to Matosinhos, so check the timetable for the way back.

stops.note: Parque da Cidade — Porto’s largest park, with lakes, lawns and dunes reaching towards the Atlantic. Start here before the heat.
The Matosinhos Municipal Market of 1952: rows of fresh fish and seafood and the morning auction. Look into the hall that has traded since six in the morning.
The Matosinhos town hall and the square before it. From here you can see how a fishing village became a city.
The Leça lighthouse of 1926 on the rocky point of Leça da Palmeira. A viewpoint over the ocean, the waves and the evening sky. End of the route.

legs.note: Bus or metro line A north from Parque da Cidade to the Matosinhos market. Tram 1 only reaches Foz.
A few minutes on foot from the market to the town hall and its square.
By bus along the coast to Leça da Palmeira, then on foot to the lighthouse.

boavista-teatros.name: Boavista and the Theatres
boavista-teatros.subtitle: Casa da Música, the Marta Ortigão Sampaio house-museum, Bessa and the theatres by the Batalha
boavista-teatros.description: The route runs west to east: from the new cultural centre on Boavista to the old theatres by Praça da Batalha. Begin at Rem Koolhaas’s Casa da Música, then step into the Casa-Museu Marta Ortigão Sampaio with its collection of painting and decorative arts. Boavista FC plays at the Estádio do Bessa Século XXI, rebuilt for Euro 2004. The last stretch is by taxi to Praça da Batalha, where the Coliseu of 1908, the Teatro Sá da Bandeira of 1859 and the National Theatre of São João of 1920 all stand. Check the listings in advance: in the evening these theatres stage plays and concerts.

stops.note: Casa da Música on the Boavista roundabout, designed by Rem Koolhaas and opened in 2005. Tours of the halls and a busy concert programme.
The Casa-Museu Marta Ortigão Sampaio: painting, furniture and decorative arts of the late 19th and early 20th centuries in a former villa.
The Estádio do Bessa Século XXI — the home ground of Boavista FC, rebuilt for the 2004 European Championship. The club’s history is on show outside.
The Coliseu do Porto of 1908 by Praça da Batalha: a theatre-circus under an iron dome that staged operetta, circus and cinema.
The Teatro Sá da Bandeira of 1859 — one of Portugal’s oldest working theatres, on the same square.
The National Theatre of São João: the present building opened in 1920 and became the city’s main dramatic stage. End of the route.

legs.note: A few minutes on foot from Casa da Música to the Marta Ortigão Sampaio house-museum.
By bus or taxi through Boavista to the Bessa stadium.
Taxi from Bessa to Praça da Batalha, through the centre, about 4 km.
The Coliseu and the Teatro Sá da Bandeira stand side by side on Praça da Batalha.
A couple of minutes to the National Theatre of São João.

paco-igrejas.name: The Bishop’s Palace and the Old Churches
paco-igrejas.subtitle: Paço Episcopal, the cathedral, the churches of Vitória and the Carmelites
paco-igrejas.description: A walking route through the church heart of Porto. Begin at the Bishop’s Palace (Paço Episcopal), the Baroque residence of the 18th-century bishops facing the cathedral. Visit the 12th-century Romanesque cathedral on the hill, then descend to the church of Our Lady of Victory (Igreja da Vitória) and climb to the Carmelite church with its Baroque altar. Beside it stands Carmo church, its façade clad in azulejos. Finish at the Clérigos tower for a panorama of the city. The route is short and almost entirely on foot; start in the morning, while the churches are quiet.

stops.note: The Bishop’s Palace (Paço Episcopal), rebuilt in the 18th century under Bishop Rafael de Mendonça. The façade and grand staircase are attributed to Nicolau Nasoni.
Porto’s 12th-century Romanesque cathedral on the hill: the Gothic cloister with azulejos and a terrace over the bishop’s palace.
The 16th-century church of Our Lady of Victory (Igreja da Vitória) in the Vitória quarter, with a Baroque interior.
The 17th-century Carmelite church: a Baroque altar and the quiet of the monastic quarter on Rua das Carmelitas.
Carmo church opposite: its side façade is covered in blue-and-white azulejos.
Niccolò Nasoni’s Clérigos church and tower. Climb the 1763 belfry — 225 steps and a panorama of the city. End of the route.

legs.note: The palace stands directly opposite the cathedral, on the cathedral square.
From the cathedral down to the Vitória quarter and the church of Our Lady of Victory.
North through the streets to the Carmelite church on Rua das Carmelitas.
Carmo church stands opposite, across the street.
A few minutes south to the Clérigos church and tower.
